# Case study: coastal shipping TKU {#sec-m1-estudo-de-caso} This chapter brings together everything seen in the module into a single workflow, from the raw file to the exported result. The question is a typical request from a technical team: > *Which links and which states concentrate coastal shipping in TKU, how is this > transport split by cargo profile, and what is the origin–destination matrix between > states?* The data come from **ANTAQ's Estatístico Aquaviário** (table TB6.1, TKU for 2025), in `dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx`. See [Example data](a-dados.qmd). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(stringr) library(ggplot2) library(scales) library(readxl) ggplot2::theme_set(ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")) ``` ::: ## Step 1: Read and get to know the data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-")) colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2", "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem", "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino", "tku") stopifnot(ncol(bruto) == length(colunas)) names(bruto) <- colunas dim(bruto) #> [1] 732 12 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bruto |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 3) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | ano|perfil |sh2 |pais_origem |uf_origem |cidade_origem |instalacao_origem |pais_destino |uf_destino |cidade_destino |instalacao_destino | tku| |----:|:--------------------|:--------------|:-----------|:---------|:-------------|:----------------------------|:------------|:----------|:-----------------------|:---------------------------|------------:| | 2025|Carga Conteinerizada |CT-Contêineres |Brasil |AM |Itacoatiara |IP4 Itacoatiara |Brasil |PR |Paranaguá |Paranaguá | 4213386.6| | 2025|Carga Conteinerizada |CT-Contêineres |Brasil |AM |Itacoatiara |Terminais Fluviais do Brasil |Brasil |CE |São Gonçalo do Amarante |Terminal Portuário do Pecém | 725465.9| | 2025|Carga Conteinerizada |CT-Contêineres |Brasil |AM |Manaus |Manaus |Brasil |SP |Guarujá |Santos | 8332538649.4| ::: ::: Three questions before any calculation. **1. What is the unit of observation?** The hypothesis is "one pair of facilities per commodity"; the test shows that one dimension is missing: the cargo profile. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c( linhas = nrow(bruto), inst_inst_sh2 = nrow(dplyr::distinct(bruto, instalacao_origem, instalacao_destino, sh2)), mais_perfil = nrow(dplyr::distinct(bruto, perfil, sh2, instalacao_origem, instalacao_destino)) ) #> linhas inst_inst_sh2 mais_perfil #> 732 674 732 ``` ::: The key is *profile × commodity × origin facility × destination facility*, and it is what allows TKU to be summed in broader aggregations. **2. Do the data cover what is expected?** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bruto |> dplyr::summarise( ano_min = min(ano), ano_max = max(ano), paises = dplyr::n_distinct(c(pais_origem, pais_destino), na.rm = TRUE), ufs_destino = dplyr::n_distinct(uf_destino, na.rm = TRUE), sh2 = dplyr::n_distinct(sh2) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: **3. Are there missing or impossible values?** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c( na_tku = sum(is.na(bruto$tku)), tku_zero = sum(bruto$tku == 0), tku_negativo = sum(bruto$tku < 0), na_uf_origem = sum(is.na(bruto$uf_origem)) ) #> na_tku tku_zero tku_negativo na_uf_origem #> 0 132 0 120 ``` ::: The 132 records with zero TKU and the 120 rows without identification are the subject of @sec-m1-limpeza: they are combinations of profile and commodity **with no flow** in the period. ## Step 2: Clean and standardise ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cabotagem <- bruto |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |> dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |> dplyr::mutate( uf_origem = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem), uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino), tku_bi = tku / 1e9, tipo_ligacao = dplyr::case_when( uf_origem == "ZEE/PLAT. CONTINENTAL" ~ "offshore", uf_origem == "INDETERMINADO" ~ "indeterminada", uf_origem == uf_destino ~ "intraestadual", .default = "interestadual" ), origem = dplyr::if_else(tipo_ligacao == "offshore", "ZEE/Plataforma Continental", stringr::str_c(cidade_origem, " (", uf_origem, ")")), destino = stringr::str_c(cidade_destino, " (", uf_destino, ")") ) stopifnot(nrow(cabotagem) == 600, all(cabotagem$tku > 0)) dplyr::glimpse(cabotagem) #> Rows: 600 #> Columns: 16 #> $ ano 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 202… #> $ perfil "Carga Conteinerizada", "Carga Conteinerizada", "Ca… #> $ sh2 "CT-Contêineres", "CT-Contêineres", "CT-Contêineres… #> $ pais_origem "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "… #> $ uf_origem "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM… #> $ cidade_origem "Itacoatiara", "Itacoatiara", "Manaus", "Manaus", "… #> $ instalacao_origem "IP4 Itacoatiara", "Terminais Fluviais do Brasil", … #> $ pais_destino "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "… #> $ uf_destino "PR", "CE", "SP", "BA", "RJ", "PE", "CE", "PR", "SC… #> $ cidade_destino "Paranaguá", "São Gonçalo do Amarante", "Guarujá", … #> $ instalacao_destino "Paranaguá", "Terminal Portuário do Pecém", "Santos… #> $ tku 4213386.6, 725465.9, 8332538649.4, 1600854068.7, 15… #> $ tku_bi 0.0042133866, 0.0007254659, 8.3325386494, 1.6008540… #> $ tipo_ligacao "interestadual", "interestadual", "interestadual", … #> $ origem "Itacoatiara (AM)", "Itacoatiara (AM)", "Manaus (AM… #> $ destino "Paranaguá (PR)", "São Gonçalo do Amarante (CE)", "… ``` ::: ## Step 3: The big picture ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} panorama <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise( ligacoes = dplyr::n(), instalacoes = dplyr::n_distinct(c(instalacao_origem, instalacao_destino), na.rm = TRUE), municipios = dplyr::n_distinct(c(cidade_origem, cidade_destino), na.rm = TRUE), mercadorias = dplyr::n_distinct(sh2), tku_total_bi = round(sum(tku_bi), 1), tku_mediano_mi = round(median(tku) / 1e6, 1) ) panorama |> t() |> knitr::kable(col.names = "value") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | value| |:--------------|-----:| |ligacoes | 600.0| |instalacoes | 120.0| |municipios | 57.0| |mercadorias | 23.0| |tku_total_bi | 286.9| |tku_mediano_mi | 59.7| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} por_tipo <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = tipo_ligacao) |> dplyr::mutate(part = tku_bi / sum(tku_bi)) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) por_tipo |> dplyr::transmute( `Link type` = tipo_ligacao, Links = ligacoes, `TKU (bn)` = round(tku_bi, 1), `Share (%)` = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1) ) |> knitr::kable(align = "lrrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Link type | Links| TKU (bn)| Share (%)| |:-------------|-----:|--------:|---------:| |interestadual | 518| 166.5| 58.0%| |offshore | 37| 109.5| 38.2%| |intraestadual | 42| 10.9| 3.8%| |indeterminada | 3| 0.0| 0.0%| ::: ::: The first relevant result already appears here: almost **40% of coastal shipping TKU does not originate at a port on land**, but on the platforms of the Exclusive Economic Zone. It is oil leaving the platforms for terminals on the mainland. And, in any analysis of the port network, these links need to be treated separately. ## Step 4: Which links concentrate the flow ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_ligacoes <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(origem, destino)) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) |> dplyr::mutate( par = stringr::str_c(origem, " → ", destino), part = tku_bi / sum(tku_bi), part_acum = cumsum(part) ) top_ligacoes |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) |> dplyr::transmute( Pair = par, `TKU (bn)` = round(tku_bi, 2), `Share (%)` = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1), `Cum. (%)` = scales::percent(part_acum, accuracy = 0.1) ) |> knitr::kable(align = "lrrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Pair | TKU (bn)| Share (%)| Cum. (%)| |:------------------------------------------------------|--------:|---------:|--------:| |ZEE/Plataforma Continental → São João da Barra (RJ) | 27.89| 9.7%| 9.7%| |ZEE/Plataforma Continental → São Sebastião (SP) | 19.59| 6.8%| 16.5%| |ZEE/Plataforma Continental → Angra dos Reis (RJ) | 17.42| 6.1%| 22.6%| |Juruti (PA) → São Luís (MA) | 16.47| 5.7%| 28.4%| |ZEE/Plataforma Continental → Madre de Deus (BA) | 15.28| 5.3%| 33.7%| |Oriximiná (PA) → Barcarena (PA) | 10.48| 3.7%| 37.3%| |ZEE/Plataforma Continental → Osório (RS) | 8.38| 2.9%| 40.3%| |Manaus (AM) → Guarujá (SP) | 8.33| 2.9%| 43.2%| |ZEE/Plataforma Continental → São Francisco do Sul (SC) | 8.16| 2.8%| 46.0%| |ZEE/Plataforma Continental → Ipojuca (PE) | 7.88| 2.7%| 48.8%| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_ligacoes |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) |> ggplot(aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(par, tku_bi))) + geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") + geom_text(aes(label = scales::number(tku_bi, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) + labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL, title = "Coastal shipping: main links", caption = "Source: ANTAQ, Estatístico Aquaviário (TB6.1), 2025.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Ten largest coastal shipping links in TKU (2025)](m1-08-estudo-de-caso_files/figure-html/fig-caso-top-1.png){#fig-caso-top width=1200} ::: ::: How many links account for 80% of the TKU? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n80 <- sum(top_ligacoes$part_acum < 0.80) + 1 c(ligacoes_ate_80pct = n80, total_de_ligacoes = nrow(top_ligacoes), proporcao = round(n80 / nrow(top_ligacoes), 3)) #> ligacoes_ate_80pct total_de_ligacoes proporcao #> 56.000 426.000 0.131 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_ligacoes |> dplyr::mutate(i = dplyr::row_number() / dplyr::n()) |> ggplot(aes(x = i, y = part_acum)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#1a5b8a") + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#e07b39") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) + labs(x = "OD links (ordered by TKU)", y = "Cumulative TKU") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Concentration of TKU: cumulative share by ordered link](m1-08-estudo-de-caso_files/figure-html/fig-caso-concentracao-1.png){#fig-caso-concentracao width=1200} ::: ::: This curve is the strongest technical argument to be drawn from the dataset: **about 13% of the municipal pairs concentrate 80% of the TKU**. The dashed line is the line of equality. If every pair had the same TKU, the curve would coincide with it. ## Step 5: Cargo profile ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} por_perfil <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), ligacoes = dplyr::n(), .by = perfil) |> dplyr::mutate(part = tku_bi / sum(tku_bi)) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) por_perfil |> dplyr::transmute( Profile = perfil, `TKU (bn)` = round(tku_bi, 1), `Share "resultados/matriz_od_longo.csv") saveRDS(cabotagem, "dados/cabotagem_limpa.rds") ``` ::: The whole script of this chapter has fewer than 80 useful lines and can be run again on next year's file unchanged. That is exactly the gain that justifies swapping the spreadsheet for code. ## What this case study showed 1. The dataset has 732 records, of which **600 have flow**; the other 132 are structural zeros. 2. The table's key includes the **cargo profile**. Finding it avoided double counting. 3. **38% of the TKU is offshore**, and this category only appeared because the invalid-state check was investigated instead of discarded. 4. The system is **highly concentrated**: ~13% of the pairs account for 80% of the TKU. 5. Every result came from a script that can be run again, with checks that fail loudly if the next version of the dataset changes structure. ## Challenge: Comex Stat exports To practise on your own, the same workflow applied to a **large** dataset. Comex Stat (Brazil's foreign trade statistics) publishes municipal export and import data as open CSV: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. download (a file of hundreds of MB; do it once and keep it) dir.create("dados/brutos", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE) url_exp <- "https://balanca.economia.gov.br/balanca/bd/comexstat-bd/mun/EXP_2025_MUN.csv" destino <- "dados/brutos/EXP_2025_MUN.csv" if (!file.exists(destino)) download.file(url_exp, destino, mode = "wb") # lookup tables (municipalities and NCM) download.file("https://balanca.economia.gov.br/balanca/bd/tabelas/UF_MUN.csv", "dados/brutos/UF_MUN.csv", mode = "wb") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 2. lazy reading with duckplyr: only the aggregate comes into memory library(duckplyr) exp_mun <- duckplyr::read_csv_duckdb( "dados/brutos/EXP_2025_MUN.csv", options = list(delim = ";", header = TRUE) ) por_municipio <- exp_mun |> dplyr::summarise( valor_fob = sum(VL_FOB, na.rm = TRUE), peso_kg = sum(KG_LIQUIDO, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(SH4, CO_MUN) ) |> dplyr::collect() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 3. performance comparison: duckplyr x data.table x readr system.time({ a <- duckplyr::read_csv_duckdb("dados/brutos/EXP_2025_MUN.csv", options = list(delim = ";")) |> dplyr::summarise(v = sum(VL_FOB), .by = CO_MUN) |> dplyr::collect() }) system.time({ b <- data.table::fread("dados/brutos/EXP_2025_MUN.csv")[, .(v = sum(VL_FOB)), by = CO_MUN] }) system.time({ d <- readr::read_csv2("dados/brutos/EXP_2025_MUN.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> dplyr::summarise(v = sum(VL_FOB), .by = CO_MUN) }) ``` ::: What you should produce: 1. The 20 commodities (HS4) with the highest FOB value exported in 2025. 2. The 20 municipalities with the highest exported value, with name and state (`join` with `UF_MUN.csv`). 3. A bar chart of the top 10 municipalities, with the axis formatted in billions of US$. 4. A cross table of FOB value by state and by HS chapter. 5. The processing time of the three approaches in item 3 above, with a sentence explaining the difference. ::: {.callout-tip} Comex Stat's `CO_MUN` has **6 digits** (the municipality code without the check digit), while IBGE and `geobr` use **7**. That is the kind of detail that breaks a join and that we discuss in module 2, when these municipalities need to become geometries on the map. :::
